specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically coherent argument for the necessity and effectiveness of contextualized word representations for detecting lexical entailment. It clearly articulates the problem of context-agnostic approaches, proposes a novel method for contextualization using masked representations, and systematically evaluates its performance across multiple datasets, including two newly introduced ones. The paper's structure moves from problem definition to proposed solution, detailed methodology, empirical results, and a focused analysis of key hypotheses. The reasoning generally strengthens through empirical validation, particularly in demonstrating improvements over baselines and the superiority of the proposed masking technique. However, the explicit limitation of 'entailment' to 'specificity relation' in Section 2, while a clear operational choice, creates a slight tension with the broader problem statement in the introduction, which implies a wider scope for lexical entailment. The reliance on pre-trained embeddings and limited classifier tuning are acknowledged operational assumptions, but their potential impact on the generalizability of the features could be further explored.
logical_argument_graph: Problem Statement (Section 1): Lexical entailment is crucial for NLP, but prior work largely ignores context, leading to ambiguities (e.g., 'game' example). Entailment is inherently context-dependent.

Proposed Solution - Core Idea (Section 1, 3): To address context-dependency, the paper proposes transforming context-agnostic word embeddings into 'contextualized representations' that highlight salient context properties. This is achieved through novel 'masked representations' using column-wise maximum, minimum, and mean operations over context word vectors (Section 3.1). These are combined with semantic similarity features (Section 4).

Alternative Contextualization (Section 3.2): Context2Vec is introduced as an existing alternative for embedding words and contexts in a shared space, serving as a comparative baseline for contextualization strategies.

Prediction Model (Section 4.1): A supervised Logistic Regression classifier is used, taking concatenated word/context representations and similarity features as input. The model is hypothesized to learn asymmetric entailment behavior.

Feature Set (Section 4.2): Various similarity measures (cosine, dot product, Euclidean distance) are applied to contextualized word representations, Context2Vec representations, and context-to-context similarities to capture non-directional relatedness.

Evaluation Framework - Datasets (Section 5): The models are evaluated on three datasets: 1) CONTEXT-PPDB (Section 5.1), an existing dataset for semantic relations in context, used for state-of-the-art comparison. 2) CONTEXT-WN (Section 5.2), a novel, large-scale, automatically extracted dataset from WordNet, specifically designed for controlled analysis of context sensitivity and entailment directionality. 3) A novel cross-lingual (English-French) dataset (Section 5.3), created via crowdsourcing, to test generalizability.

Experimental Setup (Section 6): Details are provided on the use of pre-trained embeddings (GloVe, Context2Vec, BiVec, BiCVM) and the Logistic Regression classifier configuration (including class weights for unbalanced data).

Results - Empirical Validation (Section 7): Empirical results demonstrate that: 1) On CONTEXT-PPDB (Section 7.1), proposed methods (contextualized representations + similarity features) significantly improve performance and achieve a new state-of-the-art. Masked representations are shown to be superior to direct Context2Vec context. 2) On CONTEXT-WN (Section 7.2), similar performance trends are observed, with smaller absolute gains attributed to the dataset's challenging design. Masked representations again outperform direct Context2Vec context. 3) On the cross-lingual dataset (Section 7.3), context-aware features consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the generalizable nature of the features.

Analysis - Hypothesis Testing (Section 8): Dedicated analyses further test underlying assumptions: 1) Context Sensitivity (Section 8.1): Models with context-aware features consistently perform better on Macro-F1, confirming sensitivity to context changes. Direct Context2Vec context, while poor overall, shows strong context sensitivity. 2) Entailment Directionality (Section 8.2): Context features improve directionality detection without hindering context detection. Masked representations are superior for directionality. 3) Masked Representations Superiority (Section 8.3): Empirical comparison confirms that max/min/mean masked representations outperform simpler context averaging methods (mean only) for overall F1 and directionality.

Conclusion (Section 10): The paper concludes that contextualized word representations constructed by transforming context-agnostic representations, combined with word-context similarity features, lead to significant improvements in lexical entailment detection in context, are effective across languages, and are sensitive to context and entailment directionality.

strengths.title: Clear Problem Statement and Motivation
strengths.description: The paper effectively highlights the limitations of context-agnostic lexical entailment and provides compelling examples to motivate the need for context-aware approaches, establishing a strong foundation for the proposed work.
evidence: While prior work has defined lexical entailment as a relation between word types (Turney and Mohammad, 2013), we argue entailment relations are better defined when illustrating word meaning with an example in context. Ignoring context is problematic since entailment might hold between some senses of the words, but not others. Consider the word game in two distinct contexts: 1. The championship game was played in NYC. 2. The hunters were interested in the big game. Given the sentence, Carlsen is the world chess champion, chess =⇒ game as used in the first context, while chess 6=⇒ game in the second context.

concerns.title: Limited Scope of Lexical Entailment Definition
concerns.description: The paper explicitly limits lexical entailment to the 'specificity relation' (hypernymy/hyponymy) to better understand the impact of context (Assumption A1). While this provides a clear operational scope, it narrows the generalizability of the proposed method to the broader range of lexical entailment relations (e.g., meronymy, cause-effect) that the introduction initially implies are relevant for NLP applications. This creates a slight disconnect between the broad problem statement and the specific solution's applicability.
evidence: However, we limit entailment to the specificity relation in this work to better understand the impact of context.
Zhitomirsky-Geffet and Dagan (2009) formalize lexical entailment as a substitutional relationship, which encompasses synonymy, hypernymy, some meronymy relations, and also cause-effect relations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify in the introduction that while lexical entailment can be broad, this paper specifically focuses on the specificity relation, or discuss how the proposed method might extend to other entailment types.

concerns.title: Reliance on Pre-trained Embeddings and Limited Tuning
concerns.description: The method heavily relies on various pre-trained word embeddings (GloVe, Context2Vec, BiVec, BiCVM) and uses Logistic Regression with minimal parameter tuning (only class weights). While common practice, this means the performance is inherently tied to the quality and biases of these external resources and the simplicity of the classifier. It's unclear if the reported gains are maximized or if different base embeddings or a more tuned/complex classifier could yield further improvements, potentially understating the full capability of the proposed features.
evidence: We use 50 dimensional off-the-shelf GloVe embeddings (Pennington et al., 2014) to create ~wl, ~wr, Cl, and Cr.
To obtain the Context2Vec representations ~wl,c2v, ~wl,c2v, ~cl,c2v, and ~cr,c2v, we use an existing model trained on the ukWaC corpus (Ferraresi et al., 2006).

We use Logistic Regression as our classifier for both tasks, to allow for direct comparisons with previous work. We do not tune parameters of the classifier, except for adding class weights in the CONTEXT-WN experiments to account for the unbalanced data.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper addresses the task of detecting lexical entailment in context, arguing that context-agnostic approaches are insufficient. It proposes a novel method for creating contextualized word representations by applying max, min, and mean operations over context word embeddings, which are then element-wise multiplied with the target word's context-agnostic representation. These 'masked' representations are combined with various similarity features and fed into a Logistic Regression classifier. The methodology is evaluated on three datasets: an existing one (CONTEXT-PPDB) and two novel ones (CONTEXT-WN for controlled analysis of sense and directionality, and a cross-lingual English-French dataset). The paper claims significant performance improvements over baselines, state-of-the-art results on CONTEXT-PPDB, and demonstrates the sensitivity of its features to word sense changes and entailment directionality. The audit finds the core methodological choices to be sound, with strong empirical validation, though some aspects of reproducibility and generalizability warrant further transparency or consideration.
logical_argument_graph: Lexical entailment is inherently context-dependent, making context-agnostic approaches insufficient for accurate detection.
Existing context-agnostic word embeddings (e.g., GloVe) serve as a foundational starting point for word type representations.

To capture context, a novel method is proposed: 'masked' contextualized word representations are created by applying max, min, and mean operations over context word vectors, followed by an element-wise product with the target word's representation.
These contextualized representations are augmented with a suite of word-context similarity features, hypothesized to capture the inherent relatedness in entailment relations.
A Logistic Regression classifier is employed to learn the entailment relationship from the combined features, chosen for its interpretability and ability to detect asymmetric behavior.

The proposed methodology is empirically evaluated on three datasets: the existing CONTEXT-PPDB, a newly introduced monolingual CONTEXT-WN (designed for controlled analysis of context sensitivity and directionality), and a novel cross-lingual English-French dataset.
Experimental results demonstrate that the contextualized representations and similarity features lead to significant performance improvements over context-agnostic baselines on all datasets.
The method achieves a new state-of-the-art on the CONTEXT-PPDB dataset.
Specific analyses confirm that the proposed features are sensitive to word sense changes indicated by context (measured by Macro-F1).
Further analysis shows that the features adequately capture the directionality of the entailment relation (measured by Pairwise Accuracy).

The 'masked' contextualized representations (max, min, mean) are empirically shown to be more effective than simpler context averaging methods and direct Context2Vec context representations for overall F1 performance.
Despite not being optimal for overall F1, Context2Vec context representations are found to capture useful contextual knowledge, particularly for context sensitivity.
Crucially, the improved detection of context with the proposed features does not come at the cost of detecting entailment direction.
The features are generalizable, demonstrating effectiveness in a cross-lingual transfer setting.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript addresses the task of detecting lexical entailment in context, arguing that previous work, largely context-agnostic, is insufficient for capturing the nuanced, context-dependent nature of word meanings. The paper's core reasoning is that by transforming existing context-agnostic word embeddings into contextualized representations, combined with word-context similarity features, significant improvements can be achieved. It proposes a novel method for contextualization using 'masked' representations (max, min, mean operations over context word vectors) which are then element-wise multiplied with target word vectors. This approach is empirically validated on an existing dataset (CONTEXT-PPDB) where it establishes a new state-of-the-art, and on two newly introduced datasets: CONTEXT-WN (for controlled monolingual analysis of context sensitivity and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset. The paper demonstrates that its contextualized features are sensitive to word sense changes and adequately capture entailment directionality, and that the proposed masked representations are more effective than simpler context averaging methods.
logical_argument_graph: Lexical entailment is inherently context-dependent, as word meanings and their entailment relations shift with context (Section 1, Section 2).
Prior work on lexical entailment has predominantly focused on context-agnostic word types, which is insufficient for real-world applications (Section 1).
Therefore, there is a need for methods that can effectively represent and compare word meanings *in context* for lexical entailment (Introduction).

The proposed method involves: (a) starting with existing context-agnostic word type representations (e.g., GloVe, Context2Vec) (Section 3); (b) constructing richer contextualized word representations by applying a 'mask' derived from the context (max, min, mean of context word vectors) to the target word vectors via element-wise product (Section 3.1); and (c) incorporating a range of word-context similarity features to capture non-directional relations (Section 4.2).
These features are then fed into a supervised Logistic Regression classifier, which can learn asymmetric behavior for entailment (Section 4.1).

It is hypothesized that these context-aware features will significantly improve performance over context-agnostic baselines, be sensitive to word sense changes, capture entailment directionality, and generalize to cross-lingual settings (Section 1).

To evaluate these hypotheses, the paper uses an existing dataset (CONTEXT-PPDB) and introduces two novel datasets: CONTEXT-WN (a large-scale, automatically extracted dataset from WordNet for controlled analysis of context sensitivity and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset (Section 5).

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed contextualized representations and similarity features lead to significant performance improvements on all three datasets, establishing new state-of-the-art on CONTEXT-PPDB (Section 7, C1, C2, C5).

Further analysis confirms that the features are sensitive to context changes (Macro-F1 on CONTEXT-WN) and adequately capture entailment directionality (Pairwise Accuracy on CONTEXT-WN) (Section 8, C3, C4, C17).
The proposed masked representations are shown to be superior to simpler context averaging methods and direct Context2Vec context representations for overall F1 score (Section 8.3, C7, C13).
The features also demonstrate generalizability across languages, as shown by results on the cross-lingual dataset (Section 7.3, C15).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript addresses the critical limitation of context-agnostic approaches to lexical entailment by proposing a novel framework for detecting lexical entailment in context. It posits that word meaning, and thus entailment, is inherently context-dependent, necessitating a shift from traditional word-type-based analysis. The core innovation lies in developing contextualized word representations derived from existing word embeddings, specifically through a 'masking' mechanism that employs max, min, and mean operations over context word vectors. These masked representations, augmented with various similarity features, are then used with a logistic regression classifier. The paper introduces two new datasets, CONTEXT-WN (monolingual, WordNet-derived for controlled analysis of sense and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset, alongside re-evaluation on CONTEXT-PPDB. Empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements over context-agnostic baselines, establish a new state-of-the-art on CONTEXT-PPDB, and provide analytical evidence for the features' sensitivity to word sense changes and entailment directionality. The work explicitly differentiates its contextualization method and application from prior work that used similar convolutional operations for sentence-level tasks.
logical_argument_graph: Lexical entailment is traditionally defined out-of-context, which is problematic because word meaning and entailment are context-dependent.
Therefore, a new conceptual frame is needed to define and detect lexical entailment *in context* using exemplar sentences.

To achieve this, the paper proposes a novel method for creating contextualized word representations: applying max, min, and mean filters (masks) over context-agnostic word embeddings to capture 'salient geometrical properties' of the context.
These contextualized representations are combined with a comprehensive set of word-context similarity features.
A Logistic Regression classifier is used to predict entailment based on these combined features.
To evaluate this new framework, two novel datasets are introduced: CONTEXT-WN (for controlled analysis of context sensitivity and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset.
The approach is also evaluated on an existing dataset, CONTEXT-PPDB, to demonstrate broader applicability and state-of-the-art improvement.
Experimental results show significant performance gains over context-agnostic baselines across all datasets, confirming the effectiveness of contextualized representations and similarity features.
Analysis further demonstrates that the proposed features are sensitive to word sense changes and adequately capture the directionality of entailment.
The masked representations are empirically shown to be superior to simpler context averaging methods for overall performance, supporting the methodological novelty.
This evidence collectively supports the claim that contextualizing lexical entailment with the proposed methods leads to robust improvements and a deeper understanding of the relation.

concerns.title: Abstract Theoretical Justification of Masking
concerns.description: While empirically effective, the theoretical justification for the max/min/mean masking approach to capture 'salient geometrical properties' or the 'exterior surface of the instance manifold' is somewhat abstract. A deeper, more intuitive or formal explanation of *why* these specific operations are optimal for entailment, beyond empirical performance, could strengthen the conceptual contribution.
evidence: However, while prior work represents context by averaging word vectors, we propose richer representations that better capture the salient geometrical properties of the exemplar context that might get lost by averaging (Figure 1).

Computing the maximum and minimum across all vector dimensions captures the exterior surface of the “instance manifold” (the volume in embedding space within which all words in the instance reside), while the mean summarizes the density per-dimension within the manifold (Hovy, 2015).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Elaborate on the theoretical underpinnings of the max/min/mean masking, potentially with illustrative examples or a more formal geometric interpretation specific to how these properties aid in detecting lexical entailment in context.

prior_stage_inputs: The manuscript presents a logically coherent argument for the necessity and effectiveness of contextualized word representations for detecting lexical entailment. It clearly articulates the problem of context-agnostic approaches, proposes a novel method for contextualization using masked representations, and systematically evaluates its performance across multiple datasets, including two newly introduced ones. The paper's structure moves from problem definition to proposed solution, detailed methodology, empirical results, and a focused analysis of key hypotheses. The reasoning generally strengthens through empirical validation, particularly in demonstrating improvements over baselines and the superiority of the proposed masking technique. However, the explicit limitation of 'entailment' to 'specificity relation' in Section 2, while a clear operational choice, creates a slight tension with the broader problem statement in the introduction, which implies a wider scope for lexical entailment. The reliance on pre-trained embeddings and limited classifier tuning are acknowledged operational assumptions, but their potential impact on the generalizability of the features could be further explored.

The paper addresses the task of detecting lexical entailment in context, arguing that context-agnostic approaches are insufficient. It proposes a novel method for creating contextualized word representations by applying max, min, and mean operations over context word embeddings, which are then element-wise multiplied with the target word's context-agnostic representation. These 'masked' representations are combined with various similarity features and fed into a Logistic Regression classifier. The methodology is evaluated on three datasets: an existing one (CONTEXT-PPDB) and two novel ones (CONTEXT-WN for controlled analysis of sense and directionality, and a cross-lingual English-French dataset). The paper claims significant performance improvements over baselines, state-of-the-art results on CONTEXT-PPDB, and demonstrates the sensitivity of its features to word sense changes and entailment directionality. The audit finds the core methodological choices to be sound, with strong empirical validation, though some aspects of reproducibility and generalizability warrant further transparency or consideration.

The manuscript addresses the task of detecting lexical entailment in context, arguing that previous work, largely context-agnostic, is insufficient for capturing the nuanced, context-dependent nature of word meanings. The paper's core reasoning is that by transforming existing context-agnostic word embeddings into contextualized representations, combined with word-context similarity features, significant improvements can be achieved. It proposes a novel method for contextualization using 'masked' representations (max, min, mean operations over context word vectors) which are then element-wise multiplied with target word vectors. This approach is empirically validated on an existing dataset (CONTEXT-PPDB) where it establishes a new state-of-the-art, and on two newly introduced datasets: CONTEXT-WN (for controlled monolingual analysis of context sensitivity and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset. The paper demonstrates that its contextualized features are sensitive to word sense changes and adequately capture entailment directionality, and that the proposed masked representations are more effective than simpler context averaging methods.

The manuscript addresses the critical limitation of context-agnostic approaches to lexical entailment by proposing a novel framework for detecting lexical entailment in context. It posits that word meaning, and thus entailment, is inherently context-dependent, necessitating a shift from traditional word-type-based analysis. The core innovation lies in developing contextualized word representations derived from existing word embeddings, specifically through a 'masking' mechanism that employs max, min, and mean operations over context word vectors. These masked representations, augmented with various similarity features, are then used with a logistic regression classifier. The paper introduces two new datasets, CONTEXT-WN (monolingual, WordNet-derived for controlled analysis of sense and directionality) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset, alongside re-evaluation on CONTEXT-PPDB. Empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements over context-agnostic baselines, establish a new state-of-the-art on CONTEXT-PPDB, and provide analytical evidence for the features' sensitivity to word sense changes and entailment directionality. consensus_findings: The paper clearly identifies the problem of context-agnostic lexical entailment and effectively motivates the need for context-aware approaches.

The proposed 'masked' contextualized representations (using max, min, and mean operations) are novel and empirically demonstrated to be superior to simpler context averaging methods for overall performance.
The introduction of two novel datasets, CONTEXT-WN (for controlled monolingual analysis) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset, is a significant contribution to the field's resources.

The paper introduces a novel approach to detecting lexical entailment in context, moving beyond context-agnostic methods. It proposes 'masked' contextualized word representations, derived from existing embeddings using max, min, and mean operations, combined with word-context similarity features. The method is empirically validated across three datasets, including two novel ones (CONTEXT-WN and a cross-lingual English-French dataset), demonstrating significant performance improvements over baselines, achieving state-of-the-art on CONTEXT-PPDB, and showing sensitivity to word sense changes and entailment directionality.

Strengths:
- The paper clearly identifies the problem of context-agnostic lexical entailment and effectively motivates the need for context-aware approaches.
- The proposed 'masked' contextualized representations (using max, min, and mean operations) are novel and empirically demonstrated to be superior to simpler context averaging methods for overall performance.
- The introduction of two novel datasets, CONTEXT-WN (for controlled monolingual analysis) and a cross-lingual English-French dataset, is a significant contribution to the field's resources.

- The explicit operational definition of lexical entailment is limited to the 'specificity relation' (hypernymy/hyponymy), which restricts the generalizability of the findings to broader types of semantic relations.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Second, and more fundamentally, the information encoded in distributional vectors is simply not of the right kind since “feature inclusion” for distributional vectors boils down to contextual inclusion, and there is no reason to think that a hypernym should occur in all the contexts in which its hyponyms appear. For ex- ample, bark can be a typical context for dog, but we don’t expect to ﬁnd it a signiﬁcant number of times with mammal even in a very large corpus. In practice distributional inclusion turns out to be a weak tool for recognizing the entailment relation (Erk, 2009; Santus et al., 2014) because denotational and distri- butional inclusion are independent properties.
